title: The Bonding Grotto
topics: van der Waals and Pauli repulsion

links.why: Pauli repulsion and the exponential tails of atomic orbitals; the H$_2$ bond is the QM two-level problem (bonding/antibonding).
The same Pauli principle that makes atoms repel at short distance holds up white dwarfs.

intro: Why do crystals hold together at all? In the grotto you weigh the four kinds of glue: fluctuating dipoles (van der Waals), Coulomb lattices (ionic), shared orbitals (covalent) and the electron sea (metallic). Compute binding energies and stiffness from two formulas each.

blocks.html: Five bond types: van der Waals (noble gases, molecular crystals), ionic (NaCl), covalent (diamond, Si), hydrogen (ice), metallic (Na, Cu). All are electrostatic plus quantum mechanics (Pauli repulsion, orbital overlap).

Van der Waals: a fluctuating dipole on one atom polarises the other; energy $\propto\alpha_{\rm pol}p^2/R^6$, always attractive and isotropic, so noble gases pack like spheres (fcc, filling 0.74). Ionic: long-range Coulomb dominates, repulsion only fixes $R_0$. Covalent: a bonding orbital puts charge between the nuclei; directional (diamond tetrahedra). Metallic: a collective band, non-directional.

Covalent bonds are directional and can join different elements (GaAs is partly ionic); ionic bonds join different elements; van der Waals comes from charge fluctuations (HS20 MC (j)). The script's 'R<sub>min</sub> ≈ 1.3σ' and its Table 1.2 cohesion values do not follow from its own eqs. 1.43 and 1.47: compute from the formulas.

No written-exam problem on bonding so far (HS20 MC (j) only); oral protocols asked why ionic crystals are insulators and how van der Waals arises. Low priority, but cheap points: Madelung, Lennard-Jones minimum, bulk modulus as a second derivative.

encounters.title: Bulk modulus of an ionic crystal

source.where: Ch. 1.6.3 eq. (1.47) plus a 1/R^n repulsion (standard Born model, not in the script)

encounters.goal: With $U(R)=N\big[-\frac{\alpha e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0R}+\frac{C}{R^n}\big]$ for $N$ ion pairs in NaCl structure ($V=2NR^3$), find $R_0$, $U(R_0)$ and $B=V\,\partial^2U/\partial V^2$.

steps.reveal: $U(R_0)=-N\frac{\alpha e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0R_0}\big(1-\frac1n\big)$: the repulsion only removes the fraction $1/n$.

$U''(R_0)=N\frac{\alpha e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0R_0^3}(n-1)$, so $B=\frac{2NR_0^3\cdot N\alpha e^2(n-1)}{4\pi\epsilon_0R_0^3\cdot36N^2R_0^4}=\frac{(n-1)\alpha e^2}{72\pi\epsilon_0R_0^4}$; NaCl with $n\approx8$: 25 GPa (measured 24 GPa).

encounters.title: Noble-gas crystal: argon from the Lennard-Jones potential
encounters.problem: Script 1.6.2: $U(R)=4U_0\big[(\sigma/R)^{12}-(\sigma/R)^6\big]$ (eq. 1.43). Argon: $U_0/k_B=121$ K, $\sigma=3.4$ Å (Table 1.1). Model the fcc crystal with nearest neighbours only ($Z=12$), so the energy per atom is $\frac Z2U(R)=6U(R)$ and the volume per atom is $R^3/\sqrt2$.

steps.prompt: Position of the minimum $R_{\min}=2^{1/6}\sigma$ in Å.
steps.hint: $dU/dR=0\Rightarrow(\sigma/R)^6=\frac12$. $1.12\sigma=3.82$ Å, close to the measured nearest-neighbour distance 3.76 Å (Table 1.1). (The script's text and its $R_{\min}$ column say $\approx1.3\sigma$; that does not follow from eq. 1.43.)

steps.prompt: Depth of the pair potential at the minimum, $U(R_{\min})$, in units of $U_0$.
Cohesive energy per atom $6U_0$ (nearest neighbours only) in meV.
steps.hint: $6\times121$ K $=726$ K $=63$ meV. Full lattice sums (all shells) give $8.6U_0$; experiment 80 meV. Note $U_0/k_B\approx$ the boiling point (87 K): bonding of this strength melts near $U_0/k_B$.

steps.prompt: Bulk modulus $B=v\,\frac{d^2E}{dv^2}=\frac{96}{\sqrt2}\frac{U_0}{R_{\min}^3}$ in GPa (from $E=6U(R)$, $v=R^3/\sqrt2$, at the minimum).
steps.hint: $U''(R_{\min})=72U_0/R_{\min}^2$; $B=\frac{v\,E''(R)}{(dv/dR)^2}$ with $dv/dR=3R^2/\sqrt2$. About 2 GPa (measured 2.7 GPa): van der Waals solids are soft. Copper: 140 GPa.

encounters.title: Ionic crystal: the Madelung energy of NaCl
encounters.problem: Script 1.6.3: ignoring the short-range repulsion, the cohesion energy per ion pair is the Madelung energy $U_{\rm coh}=-\frac{e^2\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0R_0}$ (eq. 1.47), $\alpha=1.7476$ for NaCl, $R_0=2.82$ Å. A repulsion $\propto1/R^n$ fixes $R_0$ and gives (standard extension, not in the script) $U=-\frac{e^2\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0R_0}\big(1-\frac1n\big)$ and the bulk modulus $B=\frac{(n-1)\alpha e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\,18R_0^4}$. Measured: $B=24$ GPa.

steps.prompt: Madelung energy per ion pair, $e^2\alpha/(4\pi\epsilon_0R_0)$, in eV.

steps.hint: $1.04\times10^5$ K per pair. (The script's Table 1.2 lists $1.8\times10^4$ K 'per ion' as computed from eq. 1.47, which does not reproduce: eq. 1.47 gives $5.2\times10^4$ K per ion. Use the formula.)

steps.prompt: Including the repulsion with $n=8$: lattice energy per pair in eV.
steps.hint: At equilibrium the repulsion is $1/n$ of the attraction: $7.8$ eV. Experimental lattice energy of NaCl: 7.9 eV per pair. The repulsion costs only $\sim12\%$: the cohesion is almost entirely Madelung (script's argument).
$V=2NR_0^3$ for NaCl; $B=V\,\partial^2U/\partial V^2$ at $R_0$. $\approx25$ GPa against the measured 24 GPa.

steps.prompt: Invert: which $n$ reproduces the measured $B=24$ GPa?
steps.hint: $n=1+\frac{72\pi\epsilon_0R_0^4B}{\alpha e^2}\approx7.8$: the repulsion is very steep, as the script says (much faster than Coulomb).

encounters.title: Why van der Waals is weak
encounters.problem: Quick fight (script 1.6.1): two neutral atoms of radius $r_0$ at distance $R$ attract with $U\approx-\frac{e^2r_0^5}{4\pi\epsilon_0R^6}$ (eq. 1.42), while two electrons at the same distance repel with $\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0R}$. Compare at $R=2r_0$ and $R=3r_0$ (factor-of-1.3 estimates).

steps.hint: Ratio $=(r_0/R)^5=1/32$: 'two orders of magnitude weaker' in the script's words, roughly.
$1/243$: two to three orders. The $R^{-6}$ law (fluctuating dipole inducing a dipole) makes van der Waals the weakest bond: noble gases boil at tens of K.

encounters.title: The 1D Madelung constant
encounters.problem: An infinite chain of alternating charges $\pm e$ with spacing $R_0$. Madelung's sum for one ion: $\alpha=\sum_{j\ne0}\frac{\pm1}{p_j}$ (eq. 1.46) with $p_j=|j|$ and sign $+$ for opposite charges (attraction counted positive). Sum it.

steps.hint: Two neighbours at each distance $j$, alternating sign: $2\ln2=1.386$. Compare NaCl 1.7476, CsCl 1.7627 (script). The series converges only conditionally: the order of summation matters in 3D, which is why Madelung sums need care.

steps.prompt: How large is the partial sum over the first 10 neighbours on each side, as a fraction of the limit?
steps.hint: Still off by $\sim7\%$ after 20 ions: the slow, sign-alternating convergence the script warns about.

encounters.title: Boss: cohesion of rare-gas and ionic crystals (constructed in exam style)

source.where: constructed from script Ch. 1.6 (eqs. 1.42-1.47, Tables 1.1-1.2) and HS20 MC (j); no written exam has a full bonding problem

encounters.instructions: Written in the style of a Zheludev problem (short parts, numbers at the end). Do it on paper, then enter the numbers.
statement: (a) [1 pt] Explain in two sentences why neutral noble-gas atoms attract each other at large distance, and derive the $R$-dependence of the interaction energy.

(b) [1 pt] For the Lennard-Jones potential $U=4U_0[(\sigma/R)^{12}-(\sigma/R)^6]$ find the equilibrium distance of a pair and the binding energy. For krypton ($U_0/k_B=163$ K, $\sigma=3.65$ Å) give $R_{\min}$.
(c) [1 pt] Treat solid Kr as fcc with nearest-neighbour bonds only. Give the cohesive energy per atom (in meV) and the bulk modulus.
(d) [1 pt] For NaCl ($R_0=2.82$ Å, $\alpha=1.7476$) give the Madelung energy per ion pair and explain why the short-range repulsion barely changes it.
(e) [1 pt] Explain why NaCl boils near 1700 K although its cohesive energy per pair corresponds to $\sim10^5$ K.

finalAnswers.prompt: (c) Cohesive energy per atom (nearest neighbours) in meV.
(d) Madelung energy of NaCl per ion pair in eV.

keyPoints: (a) Fluctuating dipole $p\sim er_0$ gives a field $\sim p/4\pi\epsilon_0R^3$ that induces $p_2=\alpha E$ with $\alpha\sim4\pi\epsilon_0r_0^3$; energy $-p_2E\propto-R^{-6}$, always attractive.
(c) $E/N=\frac{12}{2}U(R_{\min})=-6U_0=-84$ meV; $B=\frac{96}{\sqrt2}U_0/R_{\min}^3\approx2.2$ GPa (nearest neighbours only; measured $\approx3.5$ GPa; lattice sums raise $|E|$ to $8.6U_0$).
(d) $\frac{e^2\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0R_0}=8.9$ eV per pair; the repulsion is so steep ($n\sim8$) that it only subtracts $1/n$ of this.

(e) Boiling produces neutral atoms, not ions: subtract the cost of moving the electron back from Cl$^-$ to Na$^+$ (ionisation energy of Na minus electron affinity of Cl, $\approx1.5$ eV). The script's balance is per ion with different numbers; check its table against eq. 1.47.
